title: Nanotern – Ternary LLM training on consumer hardware
content:
A matched fp / PTQ / QAT comparison at 126M parameters, with honest numbers.
TL;DR — We trained a 126M-parameter transformer (nanochat-style architecture) from scratch on one consumer GPU, three ways: full bf16, naive post-training ternarization (PTQ), and quantization-aware training (QAT) with ternary weights from random init. QAT nearly matches the fp model (+0.053 bpb) while the fully-ternarized "max-compression" variant deploys at 61 MB vs the fp model's 252 MB (−76%) for +0.093 bpb. Naive PTQ is catastrophic (+0.66 bpb). All runs are matched: same data, same tokenizer, same 503M-token budget, same evaluation window. Everything to reproduce this is in this repo; each run is ~1.2 GPU-hours.
Two questions drove this:
- Can you do real ternary-training research on a single consumer GPU? (A 24 GB RTX 4090, in a personal workstation, total cost of these experiments: an afternoon of electricity.)
- What does ternary quantization actually cost when you measure it honestly — equal token budgets, equal evaluation, deployed bytes counted including everything that stays floating point?
The weight format is BitNet b1.58-style ternary: every weight in {-1, 0, +1} with a per-output-row fp16 scale, signs packed 2 bits each. "1.57-bit" ≈ log₂(3).
- Model: 126M-param decoder-only transformer, faithful
reimplementation of the nanochat architecture (RoPE, QK-norm, relu² MLP,
value embeddings, sliding-window attention). Config smoke: 8 layers,
512 dim.
- Data: ClimbMix (karpathy/climbmix-400b-shuffle), pre-tokenized
into packed 2048-token rows; validation is the held-out last shard.
- Tokenizer: 32,768-vocab BPE trained on 1B chars of the training distribution (rustbpe + tiktoken), 4.68 chars/token on English.
- Training: Muon (matrices) + AdamW (embeddings/scalars), nanochat's hyperparameter scaling system, 503M tokens = 12× the matmul parameter count (compute-optimal by the nanochat rule of thumb), 1,920 steps of 262,144 tokens, ~1.2 h per run on the 4090 (~120k tokens/s).
- Quantizer: per-row threshold t = mean(|row|), sign ±1 outside, 0
inside; row scale ‖row‖₂ / √nnz. QAT uses the same quantizer in the
forward pass with a straight-through estimator; master weights stay
floating point during training. Two variants: standard (transformer
matrices ternary; embeddings/head float) and max-compression
(embedding tables ternary too; lm_head stays float).
- Metric: bits-per-byte (bpb) on a fixed 2M-token window at the start
of the validation shard. Deployed bytes count packed signs + fp16 scales
  - all float tensors in bf16. No cherry-picked generations.
- QAT closes 92% of the PTQ gap (standard) and 89% (max-comp).
- Max-compression pays only +0.040 bpb over standard QAT and is 3.4× smaller — the clear quality-per-byte winner.
- QAT quantizer telemetry was healthy throughout: per-layer trit fractions steady at ~19% / 62% / 19% (−/0/+), no divergence, no Muon+STE instability, ~4% throughput overhead vs the fp run.
Does: at matched tokens/data/eval, ternary QAT from random init is viable on commodity hardware and lands within ~0.05–0.09 bpb of its fp twin; naive PTQ of a model this small/undertrained is not viable; quality-per-byte strongly favors ternarizing embeddings too.
Doesn't (yet): these are single-seed runs at 126M params / 503M tokens (seed-2 replicates are in flight; the repo will be updated). This is not a claim about 1B+ scale, about downstream-task quality (bpb only), or about master-weight-free training (that's the TTF experiment, next on our queue). The fp model itself is a research-grade 126M, not a chat model.
uv venv --python 3.13 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.txt
python -m nanotern.dataset -n 12                 # ~1.2 GB ClimbMix shards
python -m nanotern.tok_train --max-chars 1000000000
python -m nanotern.tokenize --split train --n-shards 10
python -m nanotern.tokenize --split val
python -m nanotern.train --config smoke --run-name fp-control            # fp arm
python -m nanotern.train --config smoke --run-name qat-std --qat         # QAT arm
python -m nanotern.train --config smoke --run-name qat-max --qat \
    --qat-variant max-compression                                        # max-comp arm
python eval_bpb.py --checkpoint <ckpt.pt>                                # eval any arm
python -m nanotern.ternary --from-checkpoint <ckpt.pt> --out tern.pt     # PTQ export
Full work log with every decision and its rationale: DECISIONS.md.
Things that occurred to the agents along the way: INSIGHTS.md.
- Architecture and training recipe: reimplemented from karpathy/nanochat (MIT) as a spec; no nanochat code is imported.
- Quantizer: BitNet b1.58-style per-row ternarization.
- Muon optimizer: Keller Jordan's modded-nanogpt lineage (Polar Express / NorMuon variants), ported single-GPU.
- This project is developed in the open by a human + LLM agents (the commit log is honest about which commits are agent-authored).

report.summary: A 126M-parameter ternary LLM trained from scratch on one RTX 4090 lands within 0.05–0.09 bits-per-byte of its full-precision twin at 76% smaller deployed size.
report.background: Ternary weight models — every parameter constrained to {-1, 0, +1} — are one of the most aggressive forms of quantization on the table, promising roughly 1.58 bits per weight instead of 16 and therefore dramatic savings in memory footprint and memory-bandwidth-bound inference costs. Microsoft's BitNet b1.58 line popularized the idea and showed it can work at scale, but almost all published results come from large clusters, multi-billion-parameter models, and evaluation setups that are hard to compare against each other. A recurring complaint is that headline compression numbers often ignore what stays floating point: per-row scales, embedding tables, the LM head, and layernorm parameters. Meanwhile Karpathy's nanochat gave the community a compact, reproducible reference recipe for training small transformers cheaply. Nanotern sits at the intersection: it reimplements the nanochat architecture as a specification, adds BitNet-style ternarization, and runs a strictly matched full-precision / post-training-quantization / quantization-aware-training comparison on a single consumer GPU to ask what ternary training actually costs when measured honestly.
key_points: Strictly matched experimental design: all three arms see the same ClimbMix data, the same 32K BPE tokenizer, the same 503M-token budget and the same fixed 2M-token evaluation window. Each run takes about 1.2 GPU-hours on a 24GB RTX 4090, so the entire study cost roughly an afternoon of electricity rather than a cluster reservation.

Quantization-aware training is the whole game at this scale. Training with the ternary quantizer in the forward pass and a straight-through estimator lands just +0.053 bits-per-byte behind the bf16 baseline, while naively ternarizing a finished checkpoint (PTQ) is catastrophic at +0.66 bpb — QAT closes 92% of that gap.

Aggressive 'max-compression' wins on quality per byte. Ternarizing the embedding tables as well as the transformer matrices costs only +0.040 bpb over standard QAT while shrinking the deployed artifact from roughly 252 MB (fp) to 61 MB — a 3.4x reduction relative to the standard ternary variant, with only lm_head and scales left in floating point.

The engineering held up. Quantizer telemetry stayed steady at roughly 19% / 62% / 19% negative-zero-positive trits across layers, with no divergence and no Muon-plus-STE instability, at about a 4% throughput penalty versus the full-precision run. Deployed byte counts include packed signs, fp16 row scales and every remaining bf16 tensor.

The authors are explicit about the limits: single-seed runs at 126M parameters and 503M tokens, bits-per-byte only (no downstream tasks), a research-grade base model rather than a chat model, and no claim about 1B+ scale. Seed-2 replicates and a master-weight-free training experiment are queued.
report.impact: The most important contribution may be methodological. By fixing data, tokens, tokenizer and evaluation, and by counting every byte that stays floating point, Nanotern sets a template that makes quantization claims comparable instead of promotional — a useful corrective for an industry where '1.58-bit' headlines routinely omit scales and embeddings. For researchers and independent developers, the practical message is that ternary training research no longer requires a cluster: an afternoon on one consumer GPU is enough to run controlled ablations, which should widen the pool of people doing this work and speed up iteration on quantizers. The 61 MB max-compression result points toward genuinely small ternary models that could run on CPUs, phones or in browsers. Regular users should temper expectations: a 126M base model is not a product, and bpb gains do not automatically translate into better chat or reasoning behavior at frontier scale.
report.tools: Start with the nanotern-public repo itself — REPLICATION_REPORT.md, DECISIONS.md (every decision and rationale) and INSIGHTS.md, plus scripts that run end to end from dataset download to bpb evaluation in about 1.2 GPU-hours per arm. For context, read Karpathy's nanochat (the architecture source, MIT licensed) and the BitNet b1.58 papers for the quantizer design. To actually run ternary models on CPU, watch microsoft/BitNet and its bitnet.cpp kernels, plus llama.cpp's 1.58-bit support. For the optimizer side, Keller Jordan's modded-nanogpt lineage (Muon, Polar Express, NorMuon) is the reference.
